content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
This work presets a neural network method for the reverse engineering of binaries. The authors, build the CFG from the assembly, extract the invoked function names and generate sequences of these function calls as they would appear in execution traces. Using these sequences, a set-of-sequences2seqence model is used to predict the subwords of the name of the procedure.
Overall, the approach seems reasonable, the performance gains are good and the application is important. The paper is also well-written. Therefore, I believe that this paper should get accepted.

* It's unclear to me how the sequences of calls are extracted. Is this exhaustive? How are loops treated?

* A comparison to a GNN-based architecture would certainly strengthen the paper. I imagine a GNN (such as a GCN) over the CFG, where the initial node states are the output of the `encode_callsite`. This would certainly be interesting and _might_ be relatively easy since the authors seem to already construct the graph.

Minor:
* p6 "LSTMS" -> "LSTMs"

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
Thank you for your kind words, thoughtful input and suggestions. You raise important questions, which we think are addressable within the discussion phase. Please see our detailed response below.

| It's unclear to me how the sequences of calls are extracted. Is this exhaustive? How are loops treated?

We extract all simple paths from the CFG. As a result, loops are essentially treated as if-conditions, creating two paths: (1) the loop is not entered and (2) the loop is unrolled once.

We take a few simple steps to ensure the number of paths stays reasonable: (a) we ignore sequences that are sub-sequences of others (for example, remove "a-b" and also "a-c" if "a-b-c" already exists); and (b) otherwise, we dynamically sample 100 different paths every iteration.

| A comparison to a GNN-based architecture would certainly strengthen the paper

We present new results for a Nero-Transformer model in which we encode the control-flow sequences using a Transformer rather than an LSTM. Nero-Transformer achieves F1 score of 40.04, which is very close to Nero-LSTM which achieves F1 of 40.6 (compared to the textual seq2seq models that achieve F1 of 19-21).

We will include a GNN-based architecture ("Nero-GNN") in the final version if accepted; we will probably not manage to implement and run this within the discussion period. Note that a GNN is limited in the number of propagation steps, which is equivalent to the sequence length in our Nero-LSTM/Transformer model. These sequence lengths can be very long (~60). Modeling these paths using pre-extracted sequences is not much of a computational problem, but propagating 60 steps in a GNN might be problematic since GNNs are usually unrolled for 2 (Velickovic 2018) to 10 propagation steps (Kipf & Welling (2017), Allamanis et al. (2018), Brockschmidt (2019)).

content.title: Thanks
content.comment:
Thanks, these responses/promises for future experiments seem reasonable to me.

The other reviewers' main concern is whether the contributions of this work is "good enough" for ICLR. I do understand their concerns, but at the same time papers with similar contributions have been published in past ICLRs. I also believe that this paper should be published somewhere, but I don't have a strong opinion about which venue is appropriate. Arguably, a compilers conference would be more interested in this work.

Therefore, I hope that the ACs can calibrate among a larger batch of papers and make the appropriate decision, noting that interdisciplinary work often has a hard time getting published not because of the quality of the work but because no existing community feels that the contributions of these works fall into its domain.

content.title: Novelty / quality criteria for acceptance
content.comment:
I should clarify that I'm not arguing that the paper is not "good enough" (and I didn't say that anywhere in my review); instead I'm arguing that I don't see the value _for the ICLR audience_, because most ICLR attendees have no inherent interest in the discussed application and there are no substantial novel insights in the paper that could be applied to another application.

I think this submission solves a practical problem using fairly standard methods, and hence a conference that is dedicated to that problem space (instead of a conference dedicated to the methods) would be more appropriate.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
= Summary
Nero, a method for naming procedures when decompiling binary executables is presented. It consists of a static analysis-based approach to extract a set of sequences of calls to (named) library methods present in the procedure under analysis, and a (mostly standard) seq2seq architecture to predict the procedure name as a sequence of subtokens. Experiments on real-world data show that the method performs well and outperforms some baselines.

= Strong/Weak Points
+ The method seems to work in practice
+ The writing is reasonably clear, and it feels sufficiently precise to reproduce the results (given enough time)
- Little novelty on modeling side (straightforward extension of seq2seq) and data extraction (straightforward application of control flow graphs)
- The central novelty in the analysis (extracting "kinds") seems to contribute very little to results (cf. Tab. 2)
- Bad fit for ICLR, as the paper is written with a focus on the PL analysis side

= Recommendation
Overall, I believe that this is an application with little novelty, and few lessons to be learned for the ICLR audience - a PL or Software Engineering conference (such as VMCAI or FSE) may be a better fit for this work. Hence, I would tend to reject this in favour of more ML-heavy papers.

= Minor Comments
* It may make sense to compare to https://2019.ase-conferences.org/details/ase-2019-papers/49/DIRE-A-Neural-Approach-to-Decompiled-Identifier-Renaming, which was very recently published (at least I only saw this after the ICLR submission deadline closed, so this is no way meant as a negative)
* page 3, second to last paragraph: "basic blocks in ," but  is undefined?
* page 4, "Combined Example": I found the writing slightly misleading here: the extracted path does not show that "(ii) getaddrinfo ... stores the results _in the previously initialized memory_" or "(iii) configure _it_ to be a TCP socket." The extracted information provides no information about the flow of information or values, which seems to be a weakness of the method.
* page 4, last par:  - this should be up to ?
* page 5, footnote 1: "each call site may participates" -> participate
* page 8: "In our approach, there is no need to manually define rules for building the graph as in Allamanis et al. (2018)" - this is confusing to me, as I believe the rules for building the call graph (and abstracting kinds!) to be manually defined?

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer2
content.comment:
Thank you for your thoughtful input and suggestions. 
We would like to clarify two points that we might have failed to communicate in our original submission.

First, the task of reverse-engineering binary executables occupies thousands of human experts who perform this task daily. While their goal is clearly important, e.g., finding vulnerabilities or defending against malware, the problem remains difficult, open, and important. 

Second, our work is the first neural approach in the field. In our work, we present a *novel representation for binary code*.  We show that our representation outperforms prior representations and textual representations. we hope that our preliminary results would open the door for more research in this field. Our representation is general, and can be used with a variety of neural architectures. As evidence, we include new results for a Nero-Transformer model in which we encode the control-flow sequences using a Transformer rather than an LSTM. Nero-Transformer achieves F1 score of 40.04, which is very close to Nero-LSTM which achieves F1 of 40.6 (compared to the textual seq2seq models that achieve F1 of 19-21).

| I believe the rules for building the call graph (and abstracting kinds!) to be manually defined?
We agree, we will remove this claim

| page 4, "Combined Example": I found the writing slightly misleading here: the extracted path does not show that 
| "(ii) getaddrinfo ... stores the results _in the previously initialized memory_" or "(iii) configure _it_ to be a TCP 
| socket." The extracted information provides no information about the flow of information or values
We agree that using data-dependencies to dismantle call-sequences into “_created_->_used_” chains is worth exploring. On the other hand, argument "kinds" were designed to capture some of these connections. In the example we show that the socket was created *inside this procedure*, as marked by kind “VAL”, contributing to the model choosing the subtoken “create” in the decoding steps.
We will clarify our explanation regarding the combined example.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper explores the problem of reversed engineering of stripped executes. The main idea is to formulate the problem as a sequence-to-sequence problem namely a mapping from a set of call site sequences to procedure names. The main contribution of this paper is the application of seq2seq models with attention mechanism to the aforementioned task. The authors evaluated their method only one dataset which they constructed themselves.

Overall, this paper is interesting because of its quite special application. However, the contribution from methodic perspectives is very limited. Furthermore, it is difficult for me to make sense of all the numbers, whether they are good or bad although the authors show consistent improvements compared to state-of-the-art methods. It also means that this paper lacks a deep analysis which will help readers to better understand the impact of the proposed method within the target domain. 

Overall, I recommend to reject this paper because of its very limited impact to the representation learning research field.

content.title: Response to AnonReviewer1
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments. Please see our response below.

| This is a special application ... but limited impact to representation learning 

We emphasize that this is not an application paper, but a representation paper. Our representation is general, and can be used with a variety of neural architectures: as evidence, we include new results for a Nero-Transformer model in which we encode the control-flow sequences using a Transformer rather than an LSTM. Nero-Transformer achieves F1 score of 40.04, which is very close to Nero-LSTM which achieves F1 of 40.6 (compared to the textual seq2seq models that achieve F1 of 19-21). This shows the critical contribution of our representation.

| The authors constructed their own dataset

We note that we *had to* construct the dataset we used ourselves as this is a new task, and older non-neural work did not release datasets. In fact, the dataset could be viewed as an additional contribution of our work, as it facilitates future research on the representation of binaries (we will, of course, make our dataset and code publicly available).

content.title: Submission update 11/11/2019 - Summary of changes
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewers for their reviews and suggestions! 
We updated our submission to emphasize the generality of our representation:

1. We added a Nero-Transformer model that uses a Transformer to encode control-flow sequences rather than an LSTM, and decodes using a Transformer as well. Nero-Transformer achieves higher recall than Nero-LSTM, but lower precision and lower F1. 

2. We added an ablation of "Nero Transformer->LSTM" which uses a Transformer to encode control-flow sequences and an LSTM to decode. This ablation achieves higher recall than both Nero-LSTM and Nero-Transformer, but lower precision and lower F1. 

3. We fixed presentation suggestions (AnonReviewer2, AnonReviewer3)
